Daraus folgt die wichtigste Entscheidung des Plans: Die Shell und das Voice-Modul werden jetzt gebaut, gegen eine zweite Tür mit Mock (api.ts), damit die UI nicht auf S6 wartet. Wenn S6 fertig ist, wird nur die Tür ausgetauscht, nicht die UI. 2 · Entscheidungen, die der Plan trifft Thema Entscheidung Warum Zwei Türen Neben engine.ts (engine-protocol) kommt api.ts (api-types): Api-Interface, Tauri-Implementierung, Mock mit Fixture „Die Gang“. Die UI kennt keine andere Datenquelle. Regel 1 aus CLAUDE.md (UI spricht nur engine-protocol und api-types). Mock macht Channels, Admin und Onboarding vor S6 baubar und testbar. HTTP über die Rust-Shell Der Webview ruft nie direkt fetch auf den Control-Plane. Tauri-Commands (api_*) reden HTTP; das Session-Token liegt im OS-Keychain, nie im Webview. api-types sagt „kept in the OS keychain by the client“. Ein Ort für Token, Retry und Mindestversion. Modul-Registry Ein Modul ist ein Objekt: id, Label, Icon, Rolle, Sidebar-Komponente, Stage-Komponente, Befehle für die Palette. Die Shell rendert die Registry, kennt kein Modul beim Namen. Skalierungsregel des Konzepts: neues Feature = neuer Eintrag, Shell unverändert. Testbar ohne Rendering. Shell-Zustand shell.svelte.ts: aktives Modul, Inspector (auf/zu, Inhalt), Banner-Queue mit Priorität, Palette. Getrennt von Session (Engine) und vom Modulzustand. Voice-Dock und Banner gehören der Shell, nicht dem Voice-Modul. Settings als Modul Einstellungen und Hilfe sind das Modul „Ich“ (Rail unten): Sidebar = Navigation mit Einfach/Profi, Stage = Bereich, Esc zurück. Kein Vollbild-Overlay. Mute muss im Call immer erreichbar sein; das Dock bleibt sichtbar (ADR-004). Komponenten Bits UI (headless, Svelte 5) für Command, Dialog, Select, Slider, Tabs, Tooltip; Icons aus Lucide. Beide MIT. Entscheidung als ADR-004 mit Lizenz, Bundle-Größe und Tauri-Check. Tastatur und Screenreader für Palette und Dialoge selbst zu bauen kostet mehr als es bringt. Styling bleibt zu 100 % bei den Tokens. Einfach/Profi Eine Eigenschaft der Settings (view: simple | pro), nicht der Module. Beide Ansichten schreiben dasselbe Schema. Konzept, Abschnitt 1 und Grobstruktur. Barrierefreiheit prüfbar vitest-axe im UI-Test; jeder Screen hat mindestens einen Test, der Rollen, Labels und Tastaturpfad prüft. Die Leitplanken aus dem Konzept „gelten ab jetzt“ und sollen nicht an Disziplin hängen. Tokens zuerst Vor der Shell wächst ui-tokens/ um das, was die Zonen brauchen (Breiten, Typo-Skala, Zustandsfarben, Fokus, Flächenebenen). Farben bleiben Platzhalter. Optik-Runde (Konzept, offene Frage 4) soll ein JSON-Tausch sein, kein Umbau. 3 · Empfehlung zu den offenen Fragen aus Runde 1 Beitreten per Einzelklick, Enter per Tastatur, „Beitreten“ beim Hover als Hinweis. Channelwechsel im Call ist Leave + Join ohne Rückfrage, muss sich schnell anfühlen. Klick auf eine Person öffnet den Inspector, nicht den Channel. Doppelklick bleibt frei. Inspector standardmäßig zu. Er öffnet für Soundboard und Person; die Shell merkt sich pro Modul, ob er offen war. Kein Flow braucht ihn. Zustände werden vor U1 nicht gezeichnet, sondern als Verhalten festgelegt (Abschnitt 5, „Systemzustände“). Lofi-Runde 2 zeichnet sie, wenn die Shell schon läuft, dann gegen echte Zustände. Optik nach U2. Erst wenn Shell und Call-Screen stehen, lohnen 2–3 Token-Varianten. 4 · Arbeitspakete Jedes Paket ist ein Task in TASKS.md, ein Branch, ein Review. Größe: S = ein Abend, M = zwei bis drei, L = eine Woche. „Braucht“ nennt die harte Abhängigkeit; alles davor kann mit Mock-Daten fertig werden. U0 · Fundament (S, braucht nichts) ADR-004: Bits UI + Lucide; npm-Abhängigkeiten in apps/desktop. ui-tokens/ v1: rail-width, inspector-width, Typo-Skala (xs…xl), line-height, color-focus, Zustandsfarben speaking, muted, ptt, offline, away, Flächen surface-sunken, Motion (duration-fast, duration-normal). Dark und Light pflegen dieselben Keys. cargo xtask tokens. api.ts + mockApi.ts: Interface entlang api-types (Login per Invite-Code, Me, Channels, Presence-Stream, Voice-Token je Channel, Mitglieder, Einladungen, Rollen). Fixture „Die Gang“ wie im Konzept-Screen (Lobby, Raid-Abend, Musik-Session, AFK, sechs Leute). shell.svelte.ts + Modul-Registry mit Tests (aktives Modul, Rollen-Filter, Banner-Priorität, Befehle sammeln). U1 · Shell (M, braucht U0) Zonen A bis G als Komponenten: Rail, Sidebar-Slot, Stage-Slot, VoiceDock, Topbar mit Breadcrumb und Suchfeld, Banner, Inspector, CommandPalette (Strg K) und das Modul „Ich“ (Sidebar = Settings-Navigation und Hilfe, Stage = Bereich, Esc zurück). Der Test-Client zieht um, nichts geht verloren: heute morgen Footer mit Status, Mikro, Taub, Verlassen Voice-Dock (D) Geräte-Sidebar Settings → Einfach → Audio und Sprechen JoinCard (Einladung einfügen) Voice-Modul, Stage ohne Channel; nach U5 nur noch Fallback ohne Control-Plane Participants Voice-Modul, Stage im Call (U2 macht die Kacheln) Debug-Panel Settings → Profi → Diagnose; yappa.debug öffnet es weiter direkt Hilfe Palette-Befehl „Hilfe“ und Rail „Ich“ → Hilfe Fehlerzeile Banner-Slot (F), Priorität „error“ Systemzustände schon hier: reconnecting färbt das Dock und setzt den Banner „Verbindung wird wiederhergestellt“, disconnected nach Verlust zeigt „Offline“ mit „Erneut verbinden“. Ergebnis: ein Nightly mit der neuen Struktur, den die Gang sofort nutzen kann. U2 · Voice-Modul, Call-Screen (M, braucht U1; echte Daten ab U5) Sidebar: Channel-Baum mit Personen darunter, Zustand als Text (stumm, PTT, abwesend), Zähler, Beitreten per Klick und Enter, „Beitreten“ beim Hover. Stage: Personen-Kacheln (Ring für „spricht“, gestrichelt für stumm, Modus als Text), Aktionsleiste unten; Soundboard und App-Audio erscheinen erst, wenn die Engine die Fähigkeit meldet (Plattformregel aus CLAUDE.md: fehlende Implementierung blendet aus). Inspector „Person“: Lautstärke für mich, lokal stumm (beides gibt es in der Engine), später Rolle und Kick für Admins. Topbar: Breadcrumb „Voice / Channel“, Zähler, „Einladen“ für Admins (bis U5 kopiert es die cargo xtask livekit token-Einladung, danach einen Invite-Link). Palette registriert Channels und Personen. U3 · Settings Einfach und Profi (M, braucht U1; Protokolländerung) Zwei Schemas (ADR-007): engine-protocol::Settings v2 nur noch Audio und Senden (Migration v1 → v2, theme wandert aus, output_gain_db kommt dazu) und AppSettings in crates/client (view, theme, Hotkeys, Benachrichtigungen, Update-Kanal). cargo xtask gen-types, Snapshot der Defaults. Einfach: Audio und Sprechen (Gerät, Live-Pegel, Sprechmodus in Alltagssprache, PTT-Taste), Darstellung (Theme), Benachrichtigungen, Konto (Name, Abmelden; vor U5 nur Anzeige). Profi: Geräte, Signalkette als Stufenreihe (bis S2 sind nur „Eingang“ und „Senden“ echt, die anderen zeigen „noch nicht gebaut“), Effekte/VST (Platzhalter, Phase 3), Tasten, Netzwerk und Bitrate, Diagnose (das Debug-Panel), Updates und Kanal (Platzhalter bis Updater). Die Komponente „Audio und Sprechen“ wird so gebaut, dass U4 sie als Schritt 2 wiederverwendet. U4 · Onboarding (S, braucht U3 und U5 für den echten Weg) Drei Schritte als Vollbild vor der Shell: Name, Mikro (Live-Pegel, Komponente aus U3), Reden (Sprechmodus). Danach Lobby. Gegen Mock schon nach U3 baubar, echt erst mit Invite-Links aus U5. U5 · Control-Plane anbinden (M, braucht S6) Tauri-Seite der Api aus crates/client (Paket C1): HTTP-Client, Session-Token im Schlüsselbund, Mindestversion → Banner, Presence aus dem LiveKit-Presence-Raum → Channel-Baum (ADR-005), Voice-Token je Channel → Join. Invite-Link statt eingefügter Einladung (Deep Link yappa://invite/<code>?server=<API> plus Einfügen als Fallback). docs/mittesten.md wird dafür umgeschrieben. U6 · Admin-Modul (M, braucht U5 und die Admin-Endpunkte aus S6) Rail-Slot nur mit Rolle Admin. Leute (Mitglieder mit Client-Version und Status, Einladungen erstellen und widerrufen, Rollen), Struktur (Channels anlegen, umbenennen, sortieren; Soundboard-Sounds später), Betrieb (Server und Failover, Ereignis-Log, Updates und Kill-Switch). Was der Control-Plane noch nicht kann, ist ausgeblendet, nicht ausgegraut. U7 · Systemzustände, Update-Banner (S, braucht Updater und Remote-Config) „Update bereit“, „Mindestversion“, „Kill-Switch“ im Banner-Slot; Update-Kanal in Profi. Kommt mit dem Updater (Phase 2 der Grobstruktur). Engine-getriebene UI-Teile (keine eigenen UI-Tasks) Sie gehören zum jeweiligen Engine-Task und werden dort mitgebaut, weil die Shell die Plätze schon reserviert: Engine-Task UI-Teil Gate/VAD/PTT (S3 + Kette) Dock zeigt Modus und Gate-Zustand, Settings-PTT-Taste wirkt S2 + DSP-Kette integriert Signalkette mit Live-Pegel je Stufe, CPU und Zusatzlatenz; braucht ein neues Event (Pegel pro Stufe, ≈ 30 Hz, zusammen mit Levels) Soundboard Inspector „Soundboard“ (Suche, Grid, Hotkeys, Sound hinzufügen, Lautstärke im eigenen Stream) App-Audio Breite Kachel in der Stage, „App-Audio teilen“ aktiv, nur Windows Lobby-Radio Leere Stage allein im Channel Session-Radio (Phase 3, Vision Abschnitt 11) REC-Zeichen in Dock und auf den Kacheln (Presence-Attribut rec), Radio-Bibliothek im Lobby-Radio 5 · Lücken in den Verträgen Was das Konzept zeigt und die Verträge noch nicht hergeben. Alles additiv, bis auf das Settings-Schema. engine-protocol Settings v2 (siehe U3) mit validate und Migration. Event::StageLevels { stages: Vec<StageLevel> } für die Signalkette (Name, Pegel, aktiv), plus CPU-Anteil und Zusatzlatenz der Kette in Stats. Participant.transmit_mode ist nicht bekannt, die Kachel zeigt „Sprachaktivierung/PTT“ pro Person. Weg: Metadaten im LiveKit-Teilnehmer oder Presence aus dem Control-Plane. Vorerst zeigt die Kachel nur „spricht“ und „stumm“. Soundboard- und App-Audio-Commands kommen mit den Engine-Tasks. api-types Presence kommt nicht per HTTP, sondern aus dem Presence-Raum (ADR-005): PresenceAttributes als Konstanten in api-types, Presence { channel_id, user_ids } fliegt raus. Für die Admin-Tabelle fehlt Member { user, client: ClientInfo, last_seen }. Einladungen (Invite ist heute die eingefügte Einladung, der Invite-Link braucht InviteCode { code, created_by, expires_at, used_by }), Rollen ändern, Kick, Channels anlegen und sortieren, Server und Failover, Ereignis-Log, Mindestversion und Kill-Switch. Das ist der Umfang von S6 plus einem Admin-Teil; der Plan setzt S6 so an, dass die Lese-Endpunkte für U5 zuerst kommen und die Admin-Endpunkte für U6 danach. Systemzustände (Dock und Banner, in dieser Priorität, maximal ein Banner) Priorität Zustand Dock Banner 1 Kill-Switch / Mindestversion Verlassen erzwungen „Diese Version ist gesperrt. Update …“ mit Aktion 2 Engine-Fehler unverändert Fehlertext, schließbar 3 Verbindung verloren, rejoin läuft Warnfarbe, „verbinde neu …“ „Verbindung wird wiederhergestellt“ 4 Offline nach Abbruch „Offline“ „Erneut verbinden“ 5 Update bereit unverändert „Update bereit · Neustart“ 6 · Reihenfolge für TASKS.md U0 + U1 sofort, parallel zur Mac-Prüfung und zum ersten Abend mit der Gang. Reine UI, keine Abhängigkeit, und das nächste Nightly hat die Shell. S6 mit dem Zuschnitt aus ADR-005 (nur HTTP; Lesen zuerst, Admin danach), dann C1 crates/client. U2 gegen Mock, sobald U1 im main ist. Lofi-Runde 2 (Zustände, Lobby-Radio) läuft daneben beim User. U3 nach U2. Danach Optik-Runde (Token-Varianten) beim User. U5 sobald S6 steht, dann U4, dann U6. U7 mit dem Updater. Engine-Spikes S2 und S3 bleiben in ihrer Reihenfolge und bringen ihre UI-Teile mit. 7 · Was bewusst nicht gebaut wird Kein Mobile-Code, keine responsive Shell unter 900 px Breite. Die Zonen sind so geschnitten, dass die Abbildung aus Konzept-Abschnitt 3 später geht. Kein zweiter Space, kein Space-Umschalter. Der Platz ist reserviert, die Registry hat kein Feld dafür. Keine Hub-, Games- und Tools-Module, nicht einmal als leere Einträge. Die Rail zeigt nur, was es gibt; der Platz entsteht durch die Registry. Kein eigenes Komponenten-Kit und kein CSS-Framework. Headless plus Tokens reicht.

pages.title: ADR-001: Variant B — same core, Rust-first stack, developed outside App Hub
pages.html:
ADR-001: Variant B — same core, Rust-first stack, developed outside App Hub

Status: accepted (2026-10-07)

Context

yAPPA is developed twice, in parallel, from the same planning baseline (ADR-000):

  • Variant A lives in App-Hub/projects/yappa (GitHub crisin/yappa). It follows the baseline literally and is driven through the App Hub board (worktree per item, review lane, debate intake).
  • Variant B is this repository (D:\Projekte\dev\YAPPA). It is developed "externally": Claude Code directly in the repo, no hub.

Two copies of the same idea only teach something if they differ where the baseline itself is unsure. The baseline already names its seams and open decisions (UI framework, where the control plane lives, client shell, scripts). Variant B takes the other branch at a few of those seams and keeps everything that is the idea identical, so the two can be compared on voice quality, robustness, effort and speed of iteration.

Decision

Identical to variant A (the core idea — not up for variation here):

  • Desktop client on Tauri 2, Windows as reference platform, macOS builds along.
  • All audio native in Rust: cpal capture/output, denoiser behind a Denoiser trait (DeepFilterNet / RNNoise), gate/VAD/PTT, EQ, compressor, effect slot; real-time thread without allocations and locks (rtrb).
  • LiveKit as media plane (Rust SDK, NativeAudioSource, RED on, DTX off, fixed bitrate), self-hosted in the stages Dev → Home → VPS → own hardware.
  • The engine has a message-based API (engine-protocol) and contains no Tauri code.
  • Layering: dsp knows no I/O, audio-engine knows no network, transport knows no DSP.
  • Feature list, latency budget (70–120 ms mouth-to-ear), spikes S1–S4, update channels, diagnostics — as in the baseline.

Different in variant B:

SeamVariant A (hub)Variant B (this repo)Why try it
Control planeNestJS + Prisma on Railway (apps/api)Rust: axum + sqlx + SQLite (crates/control), one binaryOne language end to end; DTOs come from Rust via ts-rs, no second schema
Hosting of control planeRailway, separate from mediaSame host as LiveKit, one docker compose (LiveKit + control + Caddy)No Railway account; a small group needs one box. Trade-off below
Shared contractspackages/shared (TS DTOs) + engine-protocolRust crates only (engine-protocol, api-types), TS generatedContracts stay testable in one place
Desktop UIdecided by spike S5Svelte 5 + Vite + TypeScript, decided nowNo spike needed to start; same stack as App Hub; tokens keep it reversible
Scripts / task runnerNode scripts in infra/scripts, npm rootcargo xtask; npm only inside apps/desktopCargo-first repo, still no bash/PowerShell-only scripts
Work trackingApp Hub board, review lane, debateTASKS.md + branch per task, review before mergeMeasures what the hub adds by its absence

Consequences

  • Railway-outage argument changes shape. In A, control and media fail independently. In B they share a host: if the box dies, both are gone — but then there is no voice anyway. The failover story (fallback media server, channel reassignment) needs the control plane to run on the fallback host too, or as a second instance with replicated SQLite (Litestream). To be settled when stage 2 (VPS) is built.
  • Long-lived LiveKit tokens (≈ 12 h) and the client-side cache stay, so a restart of the control process still never ends a running call.
  • No existing NestJS AuthModule to reuse — auth is invite links + session tokens in the control crate (argon2 only if passwords are ever added). Small for one group, but new code.
  • Spike S5 is dropped for B; S0 here means: Cargo workspace, xtask, Tauri + Svelte shell, cargo xtask check, CI matrix.
  • Results from B are written so they can be compared with A: spike results in docs/spikes/ use the same measurements (latency per block, CPU, loopback-click latency).
  • Any of these choices may be reverted towards A by a later ADR; the seams make that local.

pages.title: ADR-002: Rust stays — alternatives to Rust (and the rest of the stack) checked
pages.html:
ADR-002: Rust stays — alternatives to Rust (and the rest of the stack) checked

Status: accepted (2026-10-07) · confirms ADR-001

Context

ADR-001 made variant B "Rust-first". Before building the skeleton, the question was asked seriously: is Rust actually the best choice, or only the obvious one? Rust shows up in two places that need separate answers:

  1. Client audio engine — shared with variant A, so this is really a question about the core idea.
  2. Control plane — variant B's own choice (A uses NestJS).

Criteria, in order: voice quality and real-time safety · LiveKit client support · denoiser and plugin ecosystem · Windows-first OS hooks (PTT, MMCSS, process loopback) · how well coding agents work in it · license fit (MIT/Apache wanted).

1. Client audio engine

CandidateLiveKit clientReal-time audioDenoiser / pluginsVerdict
Rust (cpal, livekit 0.9.4)native: the Rust SDK is LiveKit's native coreno GC, rtrb, no-alloc callback enforceableDeepFilterNet is a Rust crate (deep_filter), nnnoiseless, clack-host for CLAPchosen
C++ (JUCE)C++ SDK exists, but wraps the Rust core via FFIexcellent, industry standardbest plugin hosting (VST3/AU/CLAP)JUCE 8 is AGPLv3 or commercial; memory safety in the RT path; agents slower. Runner-up if plugin hosting becomes central
Go (pion)pion is the best non-browser WebRTC; LiveKit server is GoGC + cgo in the audio callbackOpus, denoiser and audio I/O only via cgo; no plugin hostinggood for servers, wrong for the engine
C# / .NETno native client (Unity SDK sits on the Rust FFI)GC, NAudio is Windows-onlythinno
Electron + JS SDK + AudioWorkletfirst-class JS SDKbrowser audio stack, no hard latency controlno VST, PTT needs a native modulealready the baseline's documented fallback, not a target

The deciding fact: every non-JS LiveKit client SDK (Python, Node, Unity, C++) is a wrapper around the Rust core (livekit-ffi). Any native path ends up on Rust anyway — writing the engine in Rust removes a layer instead of adding one. Discord solves the same problem with an Electron UI over a native C++ engine; Rust is that architecture with memory safety and without JUCE's license.

2. Control plane (variant B)

CandidateForAgainst
Rust: axum 0.8 + sqlx 0.9 + SQLitelivekit-api 0.8 does token signing and webhook verification; DTOs shared with the client as a crate (ts-rs); one toolchain, one CI cache, one language for agentsauth, invites and the emergency admin page are handwritten; slower compiles
Go + PocketBaseauth, SQLite, realtime subscriptions (presence push) and an admin UI out of the box; official LiveKit Go server SDKa second compiled language next to Rust; PocketBase is pre-1.0 with breaking changes; DTOs not shared
TypeScript (Hono/Fastify on Node or Bun)first-class LiveKit server SDK, fast to writetoo close to variant A (NestJS) — the comparison would teach little
Elixir / PhoenixPhoenix.Presence is built for exactly thisfourth language, no official LiveKit SDK

Rust stays. The control plane is small (tokens, invites, channels, presence), so the "handwritten" cost is bounded, and sharing the DTO crate with the client is worth more than a generated admin UI. pages.title: ADR-003: Engine seams as built, pasted invites, logging
pages.html:
ADR-003: Engine seams as built, pasted invites, logging

Status: accepted (2026-10-10) · builds on ADR-001, uses the result of spike S1

Context

Spike S1 showed the LiveKit Rust SDK carries the plan. The gang should now test over the internet with a real window instead of a command line, and every odd sound should be explainable afterwards. That forced the first real cut of the crates the plan only names (transport, audio-engine) and three decisions the plan leaves open or defers.

Decision

1. The Transport trait lives in crates/transport; LiveKit sits behind the cargo feature livekit. The engine depends on the crate without the feature and sees only the trait: 10 ms blocks of 48 kHz mono in both directions (VoiceOut, AudioReceiver/FrameSink) and plain events. The shell turns the feature on and hands the engine a LiveKitTransport. Rejected: a separate contract crate for one trait (a fourth crate to keep in step), and the trait inside audio-engine (then transport would depend on the engine).

2. Sound hardware is the AudioIo trait inside audio-engine, implemented with cpal there. The planned platform-* crates take over what cpal cannot do (process loopback, hotkeys); plain capture and playout do not need them. Tests run the whole engine with a fake AudioIo and a fake Transport.

3. Three kinds of threads. Control thread: commands, transport events, timers — may block and log. Pump thread: capture ring → 10 ms blocks → transport; not real-time, because the transport encodes on it. Device callbacks: rtrb and atomics only. The receive mix has a fixed number of speaker slots (24) so the output callback never allocates; a slot's lifetime is the lifetime of the sink the transport holds for that speaker.

4. Until the control plane exists (S6), access is a pasted invite. api_types::Invite (server address + LiveKit token) as one line of text, issued with cargo xtask livekit token. The engine command is the planned Join { url, token }; only where the two values come from will change.

5. Reconnect policy lives in the engine, not in the UI. The SDK's own reconnect comes first. If a session that was established ends anyway, the engine joins again with the same token after 3 s, 6 s, … (capped at 30 s) until the user leaves. Not when the transport says a retry cannot help: thrown out, same identity joined elsewhere, room deleted, token refused. A join that never worked is not repeated.

6. Logging is tracing, set up by the shell, with three sinks. JSON lines in a daily file (seven days kept; our crates at debug, including one stats line per second in a call), info and above to the UI as Event::Log for the timeline, and readable text on stderr. "Export diagnostics" writes one text file with version, settings and the log files. Tokens and invites are never logged.

Consequences

  • engine-protocol grew additively (participants, stats, log entries, resync); the protocol version stays 1.
  • The engine runs headless with the same code as in the app (apps/desktop/src-tauri/examples/headless.rs) — the measuring tool the plan asks for.
  • An invite is a bearer secret with a long life. Acceptable for a handful of testers, replaced by S6. Revoking one means new server keys for everybody.
  • Known gaps, accepted for the test client and visible in the debug panel instead of hidden: no resampling (48 kHz devices only — closed by A1, ADR-009), no drift compensation between a speaker's clock and our output (playout jumps when a buffer runs over, counted as "skips"), the transmit mode is stored but the microphone is always on, no DSP chain yet (S2).
  • cpal's realtime feature is on (thread priority for the audio threads); it brings audio_thread_priority into the tree.
  • Windows builds link the static C runtime (found in S1) — unchanged.

pages.title: ADR-004: Client UI — one shell, modules in a registry, headless components, settings as a module
pages.html:
ADR-004: Client UI — one shell, modules in a registry, headless components, settings as a module

Status: accepted (2026-10-23) · builds on ADR-001 (Svelte 5), decides the UI concept docs/ui/01-ui-system-lofi-v0.md

Context

The UI concept (round 1) settles a shell with seven zones (module rail, context sidebar, stage, voice dock, topbar with command palette, system banner, inspector) and modules that live in it (Voice today; Hub, Games, Tools later; Admin by role). The test client is one Svelte file. Four things had to be decided before the shell is built:

  1. How modules plug into the shell without the shell knowing them.
  2. Which component library, if any. Candidates: hand-rolled, Bits UI (headless, Svelte 5, MIT, 2.20), shadcn-svelte (copies Bits UI components with Tailwind styling).
  3. Whether settings are a fullscreen overlay (concept) or a module.
  4. How the UI reaches data that is not the engine: channels, members, presence.

Decision

  • Module registry. A module is a plain object: id, label, icon, required role, sidebar component, stage component, commands for the palette. The shell renders the registry (shell.svelte.ts holds active module, inspector, banner queue, palette state). The voice dock, topbar, banner and inspector belong to the shell. A new feature is a new entry; the shell does not change.
  • Bits UI + Lucide. Headless parts (Command, Dialog, Select, Slider, Tabs, Tooltip, Popover) from bits-ui 2.x, icons from @lucide/svelte. All styling from ui-tokens; no Tailwind, no shadcn copy. Rejected: hand-rolled (keyboard and screen-reader behaviour of a palette and a select are not where the project earns anything), shadcn-svelte (brings Tailwind and a look).
  • Settings are the module „Ich“. Sidebar = settings navigation with the Einfach/Profi switch, stage = the section. Rail and voice dock stay visible, so mute is reachable during a call; Esc returns to the previous module. Help lives in the same module. Onboarding stays fullscreen: it runs before the first call.
  • Two doors. engine.ts (engine-protocol) and api.ts (api-types + app settings). Both go through Tauri IPC; the webview never speaks HTTP or LiveKit itself. Both have mocks for the browser and tests; the mock API ships a fixture „Die Gang“ and scenes (in call, reconnecting, offline, update ready).
  • Feature slots are hidden, not greyed. Soundboard and app audio appear when the engine reports the capability. No "coming soon" buttons.
  • Accessibility is tested. vitest-axe on every screen test; states as text, not only colour; every icon-only button has a label.
  • Round-1 questions: join on single click and Enter (hover shows „Beitreten“; a click on a person opens the inspector); inspector closed by default, remembered per module.

Consequences

  • U0 adds bits-ui, @lucide/svelte, vitest-axe to apps/desktop; ui-tokens grows (widths, type scale, state colours, focus, motion). Theme stays a JSON file.
  • The UI never waits for the control plane: U1–U4 run against the mock API; U5 swaps the door.
  • The concept doc keeps "overlay" in its decision table; this ADR overrides it. The lofi round 2 draws against the running shell.
  • Revisit: if Bits UI's Command palette cannot be styled to the tokens without fighting it, replace that one part, not the library.

pages.title: ADR-005: Presence and live data over a LiveKit presence room; the control plane is HTTP only
pages.html:
ADR-005: Presence and live data over a LiveKit presence room; the control plane is HTTP only

Status: accepted (2026-10-23) · amends ADR-000 (Control-Plane: PresenceModule, WebSocket gateway) and the S6 cut in ADR-001

Context

The baseline gives the control plane a presence module: LiveKit webhooks (participant_joined/left) update a table, a WebSocket gateway pushes "who is where" to the clients, a heartbeat covers lost webhooks. That is four moving parts (webhook receiver, table, push channel with reconnect, heartbeat) for one question the media plane already answers, and it puts the control plane into a live path the baseline otherwise keeps it out of ("never in the voice path").

LiveKit has what is needed on the client side: a participant carries attributes (key/value, synchronised by the server to late joiners, meant for state that changes every few seconds at most) and can publish data streams by topic. The Rust SDK exposes set_attributes, publish_data, send_bytes/stream_bytes (livekit 0.9.6). Rooms are created on first join.

Options:

OptionPartsLatencyWhen control plane is down
A · baseline: webhook → table → SSE/WS pushwebhook, table, push, heartbeat, client consumerseconds (webhook + push)presence freezes
B · presence room on LiveKitone extra room connection per client, attributesimmediatepresence keeps working
C · poll GET /presenceendpoint, table from webhookspoll intervalfreezes

Decision

  • Every client sits in one LiveKit room presence for as long as the app runs. It publishes no media. Its attributes are the presence: channel (id or empty), app (<channel> <version>), talk (vad/ptt/open), away. Identity = user id, name = display name. Token grants: roomJoin, canPublish: false, canSubscribe: true, canPublishData: true, canUpdateOwnMetadata: true; issued at login (POST /auth/invite, GET /me), valid ≈ 7 days, refreshed on start.
  • Voice rooms are unchanged: room name = channel id, token per channel from POST /channels/{id}/token, ≈ 12 h.
  • The control plane does HTTP only: invites, members, roles, channels, tokens, GET /config (minimum version, killed versions, update base URL, LiveKit URL), and POST /livekit/webhook purely for the admin event log (join, leave, room started and finished). No presence table, no push channel, no heartbeat.
  • Where it lives in the client: PresenceLink in crates/transport (feature livekit, same runtime as the voice session), driven by crates/client (ADR-007). The audio engine does not know the presence room exists.
  • Data topics are reserved, not built: chat, soundboard (library sync by hash, byte streams), hub. They ride on the same room later.
  • Admin actions that must take effect now (kick, role removal) use the LiveKit RoomService (remove_participant) from the control plane, plus a new token policy on the next join — as in the baseline.

Consequences

  • S6 shrinks: auth, invites, channels, tokens, config, webhook log, SQLite. Read endpoints first (for U5), admin endpoints second (for U6).
  • api-types gains PresenceAttributes (the keys above as constants), PublicConfig, InviteCode, Member, EventEntry; Presence { channel_id, user_ids } is removed before it is ever used.
  • One more WebSocket and peer connection per client; for 20 people irrelevant. Attribute updates happen on channel change and mode change only (the docs warn against updates more often than every few seconds — we are far below).
  • If LiveKit is down, voice and presence are both down. That was true before (no voice without LiveKit); presence now says so honestly instead of showing stale rows.
  • A future mobile client gets presence from the same room with its native SDK; nothing server-side is Tauri- or Rust-specific.
  • Revisit trigger: a second media server with failover (phase 2). Then the presence room needs a home that survives the primary server — either the fallback server runs it, or the control plane takes presence back for the failover case only.

pages.title: ADR-006: Updates, channels and remote config come from our own box; the repo lives on GitHub
pages.html:
ADR-006: Updates, channels and remote config come from our own box; the repo lives on GitHub

Status: accepted (2026-10-23) · amends ADR-000 ("Repo öffentlich, Nightly über GitHub Releases")

Context

The baseline ties three things together: the repo is public, nightly builds are GitHub Releases, the Tauri updater reads a latest.json from there, and minimum version and kill switch come from the control plane. Two of those are blocked today: the repo is local (no CI runs), and going public waits on the logo rights question. The updater itself is the most important tool during development ("Ziel vom Merge bis zur Gang: unter 20 Minuten").

tauri-plugin-updater 2.x accepts any HTTPS endpoint: a static JSON (version, notes, pub_date, platforms.<target-arch>.{url, signature}) or a dynamic one with {{target}}/{{arch}}/{{current_version}} placeholders. It sends no credentials, so a private GitHub release does not work as an endpoint.

Decision

  • The box that runs LiveKit and the control plane also serves updates. Caddy serves https://<domain>/updates/<channel>/latest.json and the installers next to it, from a directory the release step uploads to. Channels: nightly, beta, stable. Artifacts are signed with the Tauri minisign key (private key only in CI secrets / the release machine, public key in tauri.conf.json).
  • Remote config (GET /config: min_version, killed_versions, update_base_url, livekit_ws_url) is the control plane's. The client reads it at start and hourly. A killed or too-old version is forced out of the call and shown the update banner; the control plane also refuses its token requests (version_too_old).
  • Client behaviour: check at start and hourly, download in the background, never install during a call — on next start or by click, with "Was ist neu" from the changelog. The previous installer stays local for rollback.
  • Release step is cargo xtask release <channel>: version from Cargo.toml, changelog cut, tauri build, sign, write latest.json, upload (scp/rsync to the box). First from the dev PC, later from CI on every green main build (nightly) and on tags (beta/stable).
  • The repo lives on GitHub (crisin/YAPPA, public, default branch main; the user's choice, 2026-10-23). CI (check.yml, Windows + macOS) runs there. Nothing in the distribution path depends on GitHub; the update host is our box. Being public makes the no-secrets rule binding and leaves the logo rights as the one open item.

Consequences

pages.title: ADR-007: crates/client holds the non-audio client logic; settings split into engine and app; hotkeys behind a platform trait
pages.html:
ADR-007: crates/client holds the non-audio client logic; settings split into engine and app; hotkeys behind a platform trait

Status: accepted (2026-10-23) · amends ADR-003 (settings file, shell responsibilities)

Context

Today the Tauri crate does everything that is not audio: settings file, logging, engine wiring. Phase 1 adds login and session token, the API client, the presence link (ADR-005), update checks, app settings and global hotkeys. Putting all of that into src-tauri makes it untestable without a window and ties the headless example to half of it.

Two smells in the current contracts:

  1. engine_protocol::Settings carries theme. The engine validates a UI colour scheme; the pro/simple view, PTT key, notifications and update channel would land there too.
  2. Push-to-talk is an OS hook, not an engine concern — but the concept has the engine own transmit_mode end to end. tauri-plugin-global-shortcut uses RegisterHotKey, which delivers the hotkey to our window instead of the foreground game: the game would not see the PTT key.

Decision

  • New crate crates/client (no Tauri, no audio): api (reqwest client for api-types, cache for channels and config), session (session token and presence token in the OS credential store via keyring, file fallback), presence (drives transport::PresenceLink), settings (loads and saves both schemas, migrates), updates (reads latest.json, decides "update ready", never installs). The Tauri shell wires client + audio-engine + platform-* and exposes commands; the headless example uses the same login.
  • Two settings schemas, one file each:
    • engine_protocol::Settings v2 — audio and sending only (input_device, output_device, transmit_mode, vad, denoiser, high_pass_hz, eq, compressor, voice_bitrate_kbps, output_gain_db). theme leaves. Migration v1 → v2 in client::settings.
    • client::AppSettings v1 — view (simple/pro), theme, hotkeys (PTT, later soundboard), notifications, update_channel, window state. Exported to TS with ts-rs like the others (cargo xtask gen-types).
  • Hotkeys live behind GlobalHotkey in crates/platform-windows / -macos, as the baseline's platform table says. Windows: low-level keyboard hook (WH_KEYBOARD_LL) or Raw Input, so the key still reaches the game; macOS: CGEventTap or, until then, hotkeys only while the app has focus. Not tauri-plugin-global-shortcut. The engine gets Command::SetPttPressed { pressed }; the shell translates hook events into it. S3 verifies the mechanism against a real fullscreen game and writes the result.
  • Layering rule added: client knows no audio; transport knows no DSP and no UI; platform-* know nothing but the OS.

Consequences

  • PROTOCOL_VERSION stays 1 (commands and events are additive); SETTINGS_VERSION becomes 2 with a migration test.
  • api_types::Invite (the pasted text) stays as the developer fallback; the user path is yappa://invite/<code>?server=<API> (InviteLink in api-types — the link must name the server, a fresh client knows none) via tauri-plugin-deep-link + tauri-plugin-single-instance.
  • YAPPA_PROFILE=<name> picks a config and log subfolder, so two clients run on one PC.
  • keyring 3.6 with windows-native + apple-native (C1: 4.x pulls the whole Linux D-Bus stack through its default feature); if it fails at runtime the token falls back to a file in the config dir with a warning.
  • Implemented in S3 (2026-10-23) as crates/platform with rdev 0.5: its Windows backend is exactly the planned low-level keyboard/mouse hook (WH_KEYBOARD_LL/WH_MOUSE_LL, passing every event on), its macOS backend a CGEventTap. One crate instead of platform-windows/-macos, without unsafe in our code; mouse side buttons work as PTT.
  • Revisit: if the hook is blocked by an anti-cheat in a game the gang plays, PTT degrades to "hotkey while focused" plus VAD — never breaks the call (platform rule).

pages.title: ADR-008: DeepFilterNet 3 (low-latency) is the default denoiser, built from a pinned libDF
pages.html:
ADR-008: DeepFilterNet 3 (low-latency) is the default denoiser, built from a pinned libDF

Status: accepted (2026-10-23) · decides "Denoiser-Default" of the planning doc's open decisions; follows the gate set in the vision (section 2) and measured in spike S2

Context

The vision made DeepFilterNet the default only if the whole chain adds ≤ 25 ms and costs ≤ 5 ms CPU per 10 ms block; otherwise RNNoise. Spike S2 (docs/spikes/s2-dsp.md) measured on a Ryzen 7 7700X, release build, one thread:

RNNoise (nnnoiseless)DeepFilterNet 3 LL (libDF + tract)
CPU per block, mean / p99 / max31 / 38 / 216 µs646 / 1 420 / 1 930 µs
Latency (claimed = cross-correlation)10 ms10 ms
Noise floor of noisy speech at 0 dB SNR, denoiser only−40.5 → −73.9 dBFS−40.5 → digital silence in pauses
Speech level change−0.7 dB−1.5 dB

DeepFilterNet passes both gates with room. It comes with three costs:

  1. Build: libDF is not usable from crates.io (deep_filter 0.2.5 there is years old). The git version (commit d375b2d) only compiles against tract 0.21.4 — tract 0.21.10 changed its API inside the minor version.
  2. Advisories: tract 0.21.4 brings RUSTSEC-2026-0217 (overflow in the NNEF tensor parser on a crafted model) and two "unmaintained" notices (anymap2 at build time, paste).
  3. Not Send: tract's state holds Rcs, so a DeepFilterNet instance cannot move between threads, and it allocates per block.

Decision

  • Default denoiser: DeepFilterNet 3 low-latency, model embedded in the binary, crates/denoise feature deepfilter (on for the desktop app). RNNoise stays the setting for weak machines and the fallback whenever DeepFilterNet cannot load.
  • libDF pinned to commit d375b2d8309e0935d165700c91da9de862a99c31, tract pinned to =0.21.4 in crates/denoise.
  • The three advisories are accepted in deny.toml with reasons: we never parse NNEF and never load a model from outside the binary, so the vulnerable path is not reachable with attacker data; the other two are maintenance notices without a known flaw.
  • The denoiser lives on the pump thread and is built there: the engine hands over a DenoiserKind, the pump creates the Denoiser (trait without Send). Never in a device callback — DeepFilterNet allocates.

Consequences

  • E1 wires denoise into the pump; the pump's busy-time stat (E0) shows the cost live, the diagnosis warns above 5 ms.
  • A clean release build takes ≈ 3 minutes longer (tract); CI caches it.
  • The advisory exceptions must not outlive their reason. Revisit trigger: a libDF version that builds on tract ≥ 0.21.16 — or, failing that, our own small patch of libDF for the newer tract API (Later task). Then the ignore entries are removed.
  • Weaker CPUs: 0.65 ms mean is ≈ 6.5 % of one core here; if the gang's slowest PC cannot carry it, the Profi view's denoiser switch (RNNoise) is the answer, not a lower default.

pages.title: ADR-009: Audio first — resampling, device return, loudness levelling, drift; D1 waits
pages.html:
ADR-009: Audio first — resampling, device return, loudness levelling, drift; D1 waits

Status: accepted (2026-10-23) · amends ADR-003 (known gaps become tasks) and the order of phase 1 in docs/01-vision-v1.md section 9 (D1 moves behind the audio block)

Context

The review before the first evening (docs/02-review-2026-10-23.md) listed the engine's edges: only 48 kHz devices, a lost device is reopened once, no drift compensation, no global mute keys. Which of them matter depends on the gang's hardware and habits, so the user was interviewed (eleven questions, 2026-10-23). What came out:

QuestionAnswerFollows
Hardware in the gangUSB/jack headsets, Bluetooth headsets (mic and output), audio interfaces; nobody on speakersBluetooth mics run in hands-free mode: 16 kHz mono, "phone" quality. Today they are refused. Echo cancelling is not urgent.
Weakest PCcurrent gaming PCs (Ryzen 5/7, Core i5/i7 from ~2020)DeepFilterNet stays the default without a safety net; an automatic fallback is nice-to-have.
NetworkLAN and Wi-Fi, nobody on mobile/hotspot/abroadNo TURN needed now; RED stays, jitter buffer as is.
Default speaking mode with a headsetAutomatisch (voice activation)As the concept says; the gate behind DeepFilterNet carries it.
Chosen microphone vanishes in a callswitch to the default and come back when the device returnsNeeds device-change notifications; cpal has none.
Everybody equally loud?yes, automaticallyA new DSP stage at the receiver, per speaker.
Push-to-talkhold only, no toggleNothing changes; a hold tail is not wanted either.
Global keys for mute and deafenbefore the next eveningSmall: the hook exists.
Hear my own voice after the chainyes, a button in the Profi viewLocal monitor for tuning the chain, not for the call.
D1 (updater) before or after the audio workaudio first, installers by handD1 and U7 move behind the audio block.

Options for the order were: D1 first (the review's recommendation — fixes reach the gang without a new installer), audio first, or a minimal D1. The user chose audio first; the cost is one installer file per version until D1.

Decision

An audio block A1–A6 goes onto the board between M3 and M4, in this order:

  1. A1 Resampling. Capture and playout accept any device rate; the engine stays at 48 kHz internally. A device at 44.1 kHz or a Bluetooth headset at 16 kHz (hands-free profile) joins instead of being refused. The device list and the onboarding say honestly that a Bluetooth microphone sounds like a phone — resampling makes it work, not good. Send-chain change: latency and CPU measured before and after, the resampler adds at most one block of latency on each side.
  2. A2 Device return. A DeviceWatcher trait in crates/platform (Windows: IMMNotificationClient; macOS: CoreAudio property listeners; missing implementation = today's behaviour) feeds the engine: a lost device is retried, and when the chosen device comes back the engine switches back to it and says so.
  3. A3 Global mute and deafen keys next to the push-to-talk key in „Tasten“, through the same hook; the dock shows the state.
  4. A4 Loudness levelling at the receiver. A dsp::Leveler per mixer slot: short-term level over ≈ 400 ms, target around −20 dBFS, gain within ±12 dB, moves slowly (a few dB per second), does nothing below a noise floor (so silence is not pumped up). The manual per-person volume stays as an offset on top. Mixer bench before and after.
  5. A5 Monitor. „Mich selbst hören“ in the Signalkette: the chain's output is fed into the playout mix as a local slot while the page is open; off when the page closes.
  6. A6 Drift compensation. Hold each speaker's playout ring at the cushion with a gentle, continuous correction instead of the ≈ 80 ms skip (ADR-003 known gap).

Unchanged: DeepFilterNet default (ADR-008), voice activation default, push-to-talk by holding only, RED on, no DTX, no TURN. Echo cancelling stays phase 2. The automatic RNNoise fallback when the chain tears the 5 ms budget goes to „Später“.

Consequences

  • D1 and U7 wait until A1–A6 are through; every version in between reaches the gang as an installer file (cargo xtask build, docs/mittesten.md).
  • A1 and A4 touch the send and receive paths: both get the measurement ritual of CLAUDE.md rule 5 and a realtime review before the merge.
  • A2 is the first OS-specific code besides the hotkeys; it follows rule 3 (trait, one module per OS, absence degrades).
  • Diagnosis gains the device's native rate and the leveler's current gain per speaker, so „too quiet“ and „phone quality“ can be read off a diagnostics file.
  • Revisit triggers: someone in the gang on speakers (echo cancelling moves up); someone on mobile or abroad (TURN); a weak PC in the diagnostics (RNNoise fallback moves up); the first evening's findings override this order where they disagree.

pages.title: Spikes
pages.html:
Spikes

Each spike takes 1–3 days and ends with a markdown result here (s1-poc.md, …): what was tried, measurements (latency per block, CPU, loopback-click latency), what worked, what didn't, and the decision it feeds. Use the same measurements as variant A so the two can be compared.

SpikeGoal (variant B)
S0Repo skeleton: Cargo workspace, cargo xtask check, Tauri 2 + Svelte 5 shell, CI matrix (windows + macos)

pages.title: Q: Voice quality tiers — result
pages.html:
Q: Voice quality tiers — result

2026-10-25 · Windows PC (AMD Ryzen 7 7700X, Windows 11 Home 10.0.26300) · branch task/audio-quality-tiers

Short version: five profiles from 32 to 510 kbit/s are selectable, a change during a call publishes the voice track again inside the same session (no rejoin), and the diagnosis shows what the encoder really aims at. The LiveKit Rust SDK 0.9 lets bitrate, channels, RED and DTX through; Opus frame length (20 ms), in-band FEC (on) and complexity (9) are fixed in libwebrtc and shown as facts. The profiles cost nothing measurable on the send chain — the encoder lives inside libwebrtc, outside the pump. Mouth-to-ear is unchanged per profile within the noise of the click measurement; the send rate scales as expected and RED stops working above about 200 kbit/s; libwebrtc caps Opus at about 256 kbit/s whatever is asked for.

Question

The first internet call (2026-10-24: 0 % loss, jitter 6–8 ms, 80 kbit/s with RED) sounded "almost identical to Discord". To compare on purpose, the user wants to turn the quality up in a stress test. So:

  1. Which Opus parameters can the app actually set through the SDK?
  2. What does each profile cost — send rate, CPU per 10 ms block, mouth-to-ear?
  3. Does a profile change survive a running call?

What the SDK lets through

ParameterSettable?HowNote
BitrateyesAudioEncoding { max_bitrate }asked up to 510 kbit/s; libwebrtc's encoder stops at ≈ 256 kbit/s (measured below), presumably its default maxaveragebitrate, which the SDK does not let us raise
Mono / stereoyesNativeAudioSource::new(…, channels, …); the SDK adds stereo=1 to the offerthe source's channel count is fixed at creation, so the transport keeps one mono and one stereo source
REDyesTrackPublishOptions::redlibwebrtc drops the copy once primary + copy exceed 1 kB (kRedMaxPacketSize) — with 20 ms frames above ≈ 200 kbit/s RED is silently off (measured below)
DTXyesTrackPublishOptions::dtx
Frame lengthno—libwebrtc: 20 ms (ptime); RtpParameters::ptime is pub(crate)
In-band FECno—always useinbandfec=1 in libwebrtc's offer
Complexityno—libwebrtc default 9; no SDK or field-trial path
Sample raten/a—Opus works at 48 kHz internally; the chain runs at 48 kHz (A1); more buys nothing

A bitrate change without a republish would need RtpSender::set_parameters; the sender is pub(crate) behind LocalAudioTrack::transceiver(), so every profile change is unpublish + publish of the voice track. The others hear a gap of a few hundred milliseconds; the session, the room and the presence stay.

Profiles

ProfileBitrateChannelsREDDTX
Sparsam32monoonoff
Standard80monoonoff
Hoch128monoonoff
Studio192monoonoff
Stress510 (≈ 256 reached)stereooffoff

The brief asked for „Studio“ at 256 kbit/s stereo. Measured, that is the same thing as „Stress“: RED no longer fits into the packet from about 200 kbit/s on, and libwebrtc caps the Opus encoder at about 256 kbit/s whatever is asked for — so 256 stereo with RED and 510 stereo without RED both send ≈ 255–259 kbit/s of payload. „Studio“ therefore became 192 kbit/s mono with RED, the highest step at which the redundancy still works; „Stress“ keeps the 510 request so the diagnosis shows the cap („Ausgehandelte Bitrate“ turns orange). Any other combination is one click away in Profi → Netzwerk („Eigen“). Stereo means dual mono: the microphone path stays mono, the transport puts the same block on both channels (interleave_dual_mono, a stack buffer, no allocation on the pump thread). Opus encodes two identical channels almost as cheaply as one (the side signal is zero), so "Studio" and "Stress" measure the cost of stereo, not a stereo mic.

Setup

  • Server: a second dev LiveKit (livekit/livekit-server:v1.13.8, --dev) on ports 17880/17881/17882, because the user's home server occupies 7880 on this machine (WSL2, mirrored network). Clients on the same machine.
  • Client: yappa-poc measure (crates/spike-s1, now with --stereo), 30 s per profile, one click every 500 ms over a −30 dBFS noise floor. Digital path only — no device buffers, as in S1.
  • Bench: cargo xtask bench before and after; the transport gained a bench for the dual-mono interleave.

Measurements

Per profile (digital path, 30 s, 59 clicks each, 0 packets lost)

RequestChannelsREDPayload sentClick latency median · p95 (ms)Jitter buffercapture_frame mean · max per block
32 kbit/s (Sparsam)monoon≈ 60 kbit/s57.5 · 64.839 ms13.9 · 128.8 µs
80 kbit/s (Standard)monoon≈ 162 kbit/s41.8 · 51.624 ms15.3 · 322.3 µs
128 kbit/s (Hoch)monoon≈ 257 kbit/s47.7 · 48.532 ms9.7 · 208.4 µs
192 kbit/s (Studio)monoon≈ 384 kbit/s50.2 · 51.039 ms9.8 · 131.0 µs
256 kbit/smonoon≈ 255 kbit/s — RED gone50.6 · 51.330 ms8.8 · 181.4 µs
256 kbit/sstereoon≈ 255 kbit/s — RED gone47.7 · 48.430 ms7.4 · 30.2 µs
510 kbit/smonooff≈ 259 kbit/s — capped45.8 · 46.430 ms9.7 · 208.3 µs
510 kbit/s (Stress)stereooff≈ 259 kbit/s — capped46.9 · 47.630 ms7.6 · 28.2 µs
510 kbit/sstereoon≈ 259 kbit/s — capped, RED gone48.0 · 48.630 ms7.4 · 53.1 µs

"Payload sent" is bytesSent of the outbound RTP stream over the run (RTP headers included, ≈ 5–6 kbit/s at 50 packets/s). Reading:

  • RED doubles the payload exactly up to 192 kbit/s (80 → 162, 128 → 257, 192 → 384) and vanishes at 256: a 20 ms frame of 640 bytes plus its copy is above libwebrtc's 1 kB RED limit. Hence Studio = 192.
  • libwebrtc caps the encoder at ≈ 256 kbit/s. 510 mono, 510 stereo, 256 mono all send ≈ 255–259 kbit/s. The SDK offers no way to raise it (no maxaveragebitrate fmtp, no sender parameters). The app's „Stress“ therefore really is 256 kbit/s stereo, and the diagnosis says so (Ausgehandelte Bitrate).
  • Latency does not depend on the profile. Medians sit at 42–58 ms on the digital path (S1 measured 51–62 ms), within the jitter buffer's settling; the 32 kbit/s run was the first after a server start and carried the largest buffer. The frame length is 20 ms in every profile, so nothing changes mouth-to-ear.
  • Stereo costs nothing on the pump. capture_frame per 10 ms block stays at 7–15 µs mean across all runs (the stereo runs are the lowest; the variation is run noise). The Opus work for a second channel is done inside libwebrtc's encoder thread.

A first round of the same runs with the Vite dev server and a cargo build running next to it showed 80–260 ms medians and a jitter buffer up to 150 ms — the click measurement is only meaningful on a quiet machine.

Send chain bench (cargo xtask bench, before → after)

BenchBeforeAfter
mixer: 20 speakers, one 10 ms block11.07 µs10.87 µs
5-band EQ, one 10 ms block5.35 µs5.29 µs
limiter, one 10 ms block0.87 µs0.84 µs
resampler 16 → 48 kHz, one block10.60 µs10.37 µs
resampler 48 → 16 kHz, one block11.35 µs10.37 µs
resampler 44.1 → 48 kHz, one block11.57 µs10.90 µs
transport: mono → dual mono, one block (new)—23 ns

The DSP benches are unchanged within noise; the dual-mono interleave for a stereo profile costs 23 ns per block, 0.0005 % of the 5 ms budget.

Decision

  • The five profiles ship as above; Standard stays the default (the migration maps an old 80 kbit/s file to it, any other bare bitrate to „Eigen“).
  • No 96 kHz option — explained in the help instead (glossary: Abtastrate, Sprachqualität).
  • Frame length, FEC and complexity are reported as fixed values, not stored as settings; if a later SDK exposes them, the schema grows then.

Not answered

  • Mouth-to-ear with real devices per profile (measure --acoustic needs the loopback cable, S1 rest).
  • How the Stress profile behaves over the real home server with a second person — the user's stress test against Discord is the next step; the diagnosis (Ausgehandelte Bitrate, Senderate, Paketverlust) is what to read off.
  • IP fragmentation: a 510 kbit/s 20 ms frame is ≈ 1 275 bytes plus headers, above the usual 1 200-byte WebRTC packet limit — whether the path to the home server carries that without loss is part of the stress test.

pages.title: S1: Proof of concept — result
pages.html:
S1: Proof of concept — result

2026-10-10 · Windows PC (AMD Ryzen 7 7700X, Windows 11 Home 10.0.26300) · branch task/s1-poc, on top of 6ca4d16

Short version: the Rust SDK path works. Two clients hear each other through the local LiveKit, the custom source (NativeAudioSource) and RED do what the plan assumes, and the SDK reconnects on its own after 20 s and 45 s without a link. The digital path costs 50–60 ms. Three things are not answered yet: the real mouth-to-ear figure (no microphone here that hears the speaker), a physically pulled cable, and echo cancellation.

Question

From the planning baseline ("Hauptrisiko und Fallback"): is the LiveKit Rust SDK good enough to build the engine on, or do we fall back to the JS SDK in the webview?

  1. Do two clients hear each other with cpal → NativeAudioSource and no UI?
  2. Do red, dtx and the bitrate option do what they say?
  3. What does the path cost in latency, measured with a click?
  4. How does it sound at 5 / 10 / 20 % packet loss?
  5. Does the session come back after the link was gone?

Setup

  • Server: livekit/livekit-server:v1.13.8 in Docker Desktop (cargo xtask livekit), --dev, one muxed UDP port (7882), node IP 127.0.0.1. Clients on the same machine, so the network itself adds about 1 ms (ICE round trip 0–2 ms).
  • Client: crates/spike-s1 (yappa-poc), livekit 0.9.4 / libwebrtc 0.3.51, cpal 0.18.2 (WASAPI shared mode), rtrb 0.4. Built with --release (thin LTO).
  • Publish options: mono 48 kHz, red: true, dtx: false, max_bitrate 64 000 unless noted, NativeAudioSource with queue_size_ms = 0 (10 ms blocks straight to the encoder).
  • Devices (only in the device run): capture "Kopfhörermikrofon (DualSense Wireless Controller)", 48 kHz, 480-frame callbacks; playout "Lautsprecher (Focusrite USB Audio)", 48 kHz, callbacks up to 1056 frames (22 ms). Playout cushion 20 ms per speaker.
  • Click measurement (yappa-poc measure): two participants in one process, one clock. A publishes a 5 ms 2 kHz burst at the start of a 10 ms block every 500 ms over a −30 dBFS noise floor (so the encoder has something to encode); B finds the onset in the decoded audio. This is the digital path: encoder, network, SFU, jitter buffer, decoder. It contains no device buffer, and the click is stamped when its block is handed over — a real microphone would have recorded it up to 10 ms earlier.
  • Impairments: cargo xtask livekit loss <p> drops p % in the server container in each direction (uplink of the speaker and downlink of the listener). End to end that is about 2p — the "lost" column below is what the listener actually saw. cut <s> drops everything for s seconds. Both hit the signalling connection too.

Measurements

Latency, no impairment

WhatValueMethod
Click latency, digital path, 60 smin 45.8 · median 53.2 · p95 60.6 · max 97.4 ms (n=119)measure --seconds 60 --noise 0.03
Same, other runsmedian 50.8 – 62.0 mssix further runs of 12–60 s; the median follows the jitter buffer
Jitter buffer (mean per run)30 – 40 msWebRTC stats, jitterBufferDelay / emittedCount
The max of ≈ 97 msfirst click after the joinjitter buffer still settling
Capture block ahead of the path+ up to 10 msby construction, not measured
Mouth to ear (speaker → air → microphone → network)not measuredmeasure --acoustic ran, but the controller microphone does not pick up the speakers: 2 of 18 clicks crossed the threshold, both noise
Output device latencynot measuredonly the callback size is known (up to 22 ms) plus the 20 ms cushion

Cost on the send side

WhatValueMethod
capture_frame per 10 ms blockmean 10 – 13 µs, max 79 – 328 µstimed around the call, 1 200 – 6 000 blocks per run
Source pacing, longest block interval10.6 – 12.4 mspump thread, std::thread::sleep
CPU, whole process2.20 CPU-s in 60.7 s ≈ 3.6 % of one coreTotalProcessorTime; two participants, encoder with RED, decoder, both connections
DSP per blocknot applicableno DSP in this spike (that is S2)

RED and bitrate

OptionSent (payload)Note
64 kbit/s, RED≈ 128 – 130 kbit/sserver log: track published as audio/red
64 kbit/s, no RED≈ 63 kbit/s
96 kbit/s, RED≈ 192 kbit/s
32 kbit/s, RED≈ 55 kbit/s
64 kbit/s, RED, clicks without the noise floor≈ 58 kbit/sOpus is VBR: max_bitrate is a cap, not a fixed rate

The WebRTC stats name the codec audio/opus on both ends even with RED; the proof for RED is the server log and the doubled payload.

Packet loss (30 s each, 64 kbit/s)

"Concealed" is the share of played samples the decoder had to invent — the number that tracks what you hear.

Loss per directionLost at the listenerRED: concealedno RED: concealedRED: click latency median / p95Clicks missed (RED / no RED)
5 %10.2 % / 9.0 %1.1 %8.4 %70.3 / 82.5 ms1 of 59 / 3 of 59
10 %19.4 % / 17.9 %3.2 %16.1 %75.0 / 86.4 ms0 of 59 / 0 of 58
20 %34.5 % / 35.0 %10.8 %32.5 %74.8 / 101.7 ms3 of 59 / 5 of 41
  • With RED the jitter buffer grows to 52 – 54 ms (from 30 – 40), hence the 15 – 20 ms more latency. Without RED it stays lower and the losses are simply concealed.
  • No NACKs and no retransmissions for audio in any run; recovery is RED and Opus FEC only.
  • A 60 s repeat of 20 % with a 2 s click period gave the same picture (36.1 % lost, 12.9 % concealed, median 70.9 ms, 27 of 27 clicks) — the latencies are not a pairing artefact.
  • Judged by counters and clicks only. Nobody listened to speech under loss.

Link cut (cut starts 15 s into the run)

CutClient noticesBack in the roomAudio back after the link returnedSilence in total
5 snever — no reconnect eventstayed connected≈ 1.5 s6.5 s
20 safter ≈ 14.3 s (Reconnecting)1.6 s after the link returned≈ 2.0 s22.0 s
45 safter ≈ 14.5 s5.2 s after the link returned≈ 6.0 s51.0 s
  • After 20 s and 45 s the server had already dropped both participants; the SDK rejoined with the same token and re-subscribed without any help from our code. Clicks were normal again afterwards (median 68 – 70 ms).
  • The cut is a black hole in the server container. The PC's own network interface stays up, so this resembles a dead router or uplink. A cable pulled at the PC and a Wi-Fi switch were not measured — there the OS reports the link going down, which may behave differently.

Two separate clients with devices

join --identity alice --source click --sink null and join --identity bob --source mic --sink device, two processes, 12 s: bob played alice's clicks on the Focusrite output and published the controller microphone, alice received it. 0 packets lost, 0 playout underruns, 0 frames dropped at the playout ring, 0 capture overruns. Nobody confirmed by ear in this session that the clicks were audible — the counters say they were played.

What worked / what did not

Worked

  • The custom source path from the plan: cpal callback → rtrb → pump thread → NativeAudioSource::capture_frame. The handoff costs microseconds.
  • red, dtx: false and audio_encoding.max_bitrate are honoured.
  • Reconnect, including a full rejoin after the server gave up on us.
  • The audio callbacks only touch rtrb and atomics (checked by the realtime reviewer).

Did not work, or cost time

  • Build on Windows: the SDK's prebuilt libwebrtc needs the MSVC 2022 toolset (2019 fails in abseil) and the static C runtime. .cargo/config.toml now sets +crt-static for the Windows targets — for the whole workspace, desktop app included. cargo xtask doctor checks for the toolset.
  • Outage detection is slow: about 14 s until the client says Reconnecting. For 14 s a user would see "connected" and hear nothing.
  • Bitrate is a cap, not fixed — the plan says "feste Bitrate". Opus CBR is not exposed by TrackPublishOptions.
  • The RTCP round-trip figure is useless here: 280 – 317 ms on localhost and rising from run to run. The diagnostics panel should use the ICE candidate-pair round trip.
  • The acoustic measurement needs a microphone that hears the speaker — see follow-up.

Warnings for the engine design (from the code and the realtime review)

  • No drift compensation between the network's 10 ms frames and the output device clock; the spike drops a frame when its 200 ms ring is full. The engine needs a real answer.
  • A capture backlog must be dropped, not sent as a burst (it becomes standing delay at the receiver). The spike keeps the newest block.
  • NativeAudioStream does not end when a track is unsubscribed: track lifetime has to be driven by room events. The spike leaks one playout slot per resubscribe (8 slots).
  • The SDK's receive path allocates and locks per frame — it must stay behind a ring, never in the output callback. Its internal queue (10 frames, drop-oldest) should be set explicitly.
  • capture_frame with queue_size_ms = 0 runs the encoder hand-off on the calling thread: dedicated non-real-time thread only.

Decision it feeds

  • Main risk of the baseline (Rust SDK vs. JS-SDK fallback): go with the Rust SDK. The fallback is not needed on the evidence so far. No ADR-001 change.
  • Echo cancellation: still open. Nothing in this spike tested speakers plus microphone. The headset assumption stands until someone tries it.
  • Latency budget (70 – 120 ms): the digital path uses 50 – 60 ms of it, 70 – 75 ms under loss with RED. Whether the total fits depends on the two device stages, which are not measured.
  • +crt-static on Windows is a workspace-wide build setting forced by libwebrtc; recorded here and in docs/dev-setup.md, no ADR (no layer or contract changes).

Follow-up tasks (also in TASKS.md)

  • Mouth-to-ear with a cable from the Focusrite output to its input (or a microphone at the speaker): yappa-poc measure --acoustic.
  • Second machine in the LAN (LIVEKIT_NODE_IP): pull the cable at the PC, switch Wi-Fi; listen to speech at 5 / 10 / 20 % loss; speakers instead of headset for the AEC question.
  • Find out where the 14 s outage detection comes from and whether the engine can detect silence on the wire sooner.
  • Build and run the spike on the MacBook.
  • lk load-test with 20 publishers (needs the lk CLI).

pages.title: S2: The send chain offline — result
pages.html:
S2: The send chain offline — result

2026-10-23 · Windows PC (AMD Ryzen 7 7700X, Windows 11 Home 10.0.26300) · release build · on top of main after E0, branch task/s2-dsp

Short version: the whole chain — high-pass, denoiser, gate, EQ, compressor — costs 41 µs per 10 ms block with RNNoise and 0.66 ms with DeepFilterNet 3 (low-latency model), far below the 5 ms budget. Both denoisers add exactly 10 ms. DeepFilterNet passes the gate of the vision and becomes the default (ADR-008); getting it to build cost a pinned old tract and three accepted advisories. Nobody has listened to the results yet.

Question

From the spike list and the vision (section 2):

  1. What does each stage cost per 10 ms block (mean, p99, max)?
  2. What latency does each denoiser add — as it claims, and as measured?
  3. How much noise does each take away, and how much speech does it cost?
  4. Does DeepFilterNet stay the default: chain ≤ 25 ms added latency and ≤ 5 ms CPU per block?

Setup

  • Input: assets/noisy_snr0.wav from the DeepFilterNet repository (commit d375b2d): 10.6 s of speech in noise at 0 dB SNR, mono, 48 kHz, 16 bit. Downloaded into target/s2/, not committed.
  • Chain, block by block as the pump will run it (crates/spike-s2, scratch): biquad high-pass 80 Hz → denoiser → dsp::Gate (threshold -50 dBFS, 6 dB hysteresis, 300 ms hold, fed with the denoiser's speech probability) → two peaking EQ bands (-2 dB @ 300 Hz, +3 dB @ 3.5 kHz) → dsp::Compressor (-18 dB, 3:1, 5/120 ms, +3 dB makeup, 6 dB knee).
  • Denoisers (crates/denoise): off; RNNoise via nnnoiseless 0.5.2 (pure Rust); DeepFilterNet 3 low-latency via libDF d375b2d + tract 0.21.4, model embedded.
  • Timing: Instant around each stage per block, 1 059 blocks; one thread.
  • Latency: the lag (0–50 ms) at which the denoiser's output correlates best with its input over the whole file.
  • Levels: block RMS over the file; noise floor = 10th percentile, speech = 95th.

Measurements

CPU per 10 ms block (µs: mean / p99 / max)

StageoffRNNoiseDeepFilterNet
HPF1.2 / 1.3 / 2.41.2 / 1.2 / 3.81.2 / 1.2 / 1.5
denoiser0.0 / 0.1 / 1.131.3 / 38.2 / 158.6646.6 / 1 420.1 / 1 764.0
gate0.9 / 1.2 / 11.10.9 / 1.2 / 1.80.9 / 1.2 / 1.8
EQ (2 bands)2.4 / 2.6 / 28.52.3 / 3.1 / 7.12.4 / 2.7 / 18.0
compressor5.2 / 7.9 / 25.44.8 / 7.7 / 49.14.6 / 7.6 / 12.0
total10.1 / 14.4 / 78.440.9 / 49.2 / 165.5656.4 / 1 432.9 / 1 771.3

A second run gave the same picture (DeepFilterNet mean 645 µs, max 1.93 ms; RNNoise mean 31 µs, max 215 µs).

Latency and levels

DenoiserModel loadLatency claimedLatency measuredDenoiser only: noise floor / speechWhole chain: noise floor / speech
input-40.5 / -17.9 dBFS
off—00-43.2 / -18.3 dBFS (HPF)-40.4 / -17.6 dBFS
RNNoise0 ms10.0 ms10.0 ms-73.9 / -18.6 dBFS-107.4 / -17.8 dBFS
DeepFilterNet395–415 ms10.0 ms10.0 mssilence in pauses / -19.4 dBFSsilence / -18.3 dBFS
  • With the denoiser off the noise (-40.5 dBFS) sits above the gate threshold, so the gate stays open — at 0 dB SNR a plain gate cannot help, which is why the denoiser goes first.
  • "Whole chain" floors are mostly the gate closing in the pauses; the denoiser-only column is the fair comparison.
  • Not measured: how it sounds. The three results are in target/s2/{off,rnnoise, deepfilter}.wav for listening; a 0 dB SNR file is a hard case, gaming noise (keyboard, fan) is untested. Also not measured: other CPUs, macOS.

Building it

WhatResult
deep_filter from crates.io0.2.5, years behind the repository — not used
libDF from git (d375b2d) + current tract 0.21.10does not compile (tract changed its API within 0.21)
libDF + tract pinned to =0.21.4 (as in libDF's own Cargo.lock)builds; clean release build ≈ 3 min
cargo deny with tract 0.21.4RUSTSEC-2026-0217 (NNEF parser overflow), RUSTSEC-2026-0319 (anymap2 unmaintained), RUSTSEC-2024-0436 (paste unmaintained) — accepted with reasons, ADR-008
DfTractnot Send (Rc inside tract) and allocates per block

Later additions to the chain (bench protocol)

DateChangeBefore → after (Ryzen 7 7700X, release, one 10 ms block)
2026-10-25A4: dsp::Leveler per mixer slot, dsp::Limiter at the end of the send chainmixer 20 speakers 11.42 → 13.53 µs; leveler 0.71 µs; limiter 1.09 µs (send chain +≈ 1 µs)
2026-10-25A6: dsp::Varispeed + dsp::DriftController per mixer slot (receive side only)mixer 20 speakers 14.18 → 37.34 µs (back-to-back, same run; ≈ 1.2 µs per speaker, 0.4 % of the block); varispeed alone 5.14 µs (closure-driven bench, pessimistic)

What worked / what did not

Worked

  • Both denoisers fit the engine's unit exactly: 480 samples in, 480 out, 10 ms delay.
  • The gate profits from the denoiser's speech probability: loud non-speech stays out, quiet speech keeps it open (unit tests in dsp::gate).
  • Everything except the denoiser costs about 10 µs per block together.

Did not work, or needs care

  • DeepFilterNet's dependency situation (pinned old tract, advisories) — see ADR-008 for the way back.
  • DeepFilterNet cannot be moved between threads: the pump must build it itself.
  • Its p99 is twice its mean (1.4 ms vs 0.65 ms) — fine against a 10 ms period, but the pump's busy-time stat must keep showing it on real machines.
  • RNNoise on synthetic white noise only takes ≈ 4.5 dB (unit test) — it is trained on real noise; synthetic test signals say little about denoiser quality.

Decision it feeds

  • Gate passed → DeepFilterNet 3 LL is the default denoiser (ADR-008), RNNoise the setting and fallback.
  • Send-chain latency budget: denoiser 10 ms + the rest ≈ 0 (no lookahead anywhere) — well inside the 25 ms the vision allowed.

Follow-up tasks (also in TASKS.md)

  • E1: the chain in the pump (denoiser built on the pump thread), Event::StageLevels, chain CPU and latency in Stats.
  • Listen (user): target/s2/*.wav after cargo run --release -p spike-s2 -- target/s2/noisy_snr0.wav; record a gaming evening's noise (keyboard, fan, game audio through speakers) and run it through.
  • Later: libDF on tract ≥ 0.21.16 (patch or upstream), then drop the three advisory exceptions.

pages.title: S6: Control plane in Rust — result
pages.html:
S6: Control plane in Rust — result

2026-10-23 · Windows PC (AMD Ryzen 7 7700X, Windows 11 Home 10.0.26300) · on top of 5da15d1, branch task/s6-control

Short version: the control plane works as one small Rust binary, built in well under a day; the PocketBase fallback from ADR-002 is not needed. The presence room of ADR-005 carries "who is where": a channel switch reaches the others in about a millisecond (on this machine), a late joiner sees everybody's state the moment it connects, a kick lands in 10 ms, and the token grants hold. The one weak spot is a client that dies without saying goodbye: the others see it as online for 20–23 s.

Question

From the spike list and ADR-005:

  1. Does axum + sqlx/SQLite + livekit-api carry invites, members, channels, tokens and the event log within the time box (≤ 3 days), or does the PocketBase fallback apply?
  2. Does presence over LiveKit participant attributes work — speed of a change, state for a late joiner, how fast a leave, a crash and a kick show?
  3. Do the two token kinds hold their limits: presence token = no media, voice token = no own attributes?
  4. Do LiveKit's signed webhooks reach the event log?

Setup

  • Server: livekit/livekit-server:v1.13.8 in Docker Desktop (cargo xtask livekit), --dev, dev keys; webhook to http://host.docker.internal:8090/livekit/webhook (new in infra/livekit/livekit.yaml).
  • Control plane: crates/control (yappa-control), axum 0.8.9, sqlx 0.9 (SQLite, WAL, migrations embedded), livekit-api 0.8.2 (tokens, webhook verification, RoomService), started in-process by the spike on 127.0.0.1:8090 with a fresh SQLite file.
  • Clients: crates/spike-s6 (scratch), livekit 0.9.4 Rust SDK, --release; four people (Krille admin, Ben, Sasha, Tim) log in with invites over HTTP (reqwest), then join the room presence with their presence tokens, auto_subscribe off, no media. The "killed" client runs in a child process that the spike terminates.
  • Everything on one machine: the numbers are LiveKit's processing plus the SDK, not an internet path.

Measurements

Two runs; where they differ both values are given.

WhatValueMethod
Login per invite (POST /auth/invite)3.4 – 3.5 msHTTP round trip incl. SQLite insert and two JWTs, loopback
Connect to the presence room83 – 98 msRoom::connect, no media
Attribute change A → B (a channel switch)median 1.1 · p95 2.6 – 2.8 · max 2.8 ms (20 of 20)set_attributes until ParticipantAttributesChanged at B, changes 500 ms apart
Late joiner sees the current stateyes — channel, talk mode and away present when connect returnsremote_participants() of a third client right after Room::connect
Clean leave seen by the others2.0 sRoom::close until ParticipantDisconnected at B (second run; see below)
Client killed without goodbye20.0 – 23.0 sprocess terminated until ParticipantDisconnected at B
Kick via API reaches the client9 – 10 msPOST /members/{id}/kick (RoomService remove_participant) until RoomEvent::Disconnected at the kicked client
Presence token refuses mediayes, but only after a 10.0 s timeoutpublish_track with the presence token
Voice token refuses own attributesyes, at once: NotAllowed - does not have permission to update own metadataset_attributes in a channel room

yappa-control image140 MB, release build in the container ≈ 60 sdocker build -f infra/control/Dockerfile
API test suite9 integration + 6 unit testscargo test -p control, in-memory SQLite, no network

Not measured: an internet path between clients and server, more than four clients (lk load-test stays on the board), macOS.

What worked / what did not

Worked

  • The stack. axum + sqlx + livekit-api needed no workaround: tokens with exact grants, webhook verification (WebhookReceiver), and RoomService for the kick are all in the crate. Plain runtime queries — no database at build time. One binary that is also the bootstrap and emergency tool (invite --admin, policy --min … --kill …).
  • Bootstrap without a web page. The first start of an empty database writes a one-time admin invite link to the log. Whoever can read the server log owns the box anyway, so the "tiny bootstrap page" of the baseline is not built.
  • Presence as attributes. Fast, ordered, and the server hands late joiners the full state — the client needs no snapshot request and the control plane no presence table.
  • Token limits. Both kinds are enforced by LiveKit itself, not by our client.
  • Webhooks arrive signed and become readable German lines ("Ben betritt lobby").

Did not work, or needs care

  • A dead client stays "online" for 20–23 s. That is LiveKit's own timeout for a peer without a goodbye (same order as the ≈ 14 s the S1 client needed to notice a dead link). For presence it means a crashed or unplugged PC is shown for half a minute. Acceptable for v1; the UI may grey a person out whose voice has gone silent — see follow-up.
  • A join and a leave in one server update vanish. In the first run B never saw the clean leave of a client that left within milliseconds of joining: the SDK had not yet created that participant, so there was nothing to disconnect. Harmless in real use (no one leaves within milliseconds), but the client must build its view from remote_participants() plus events, never from events alone.
  • A refused publish takes 10 s. The server ignores the presence token's publish attempt instead of answering, and the SDK times out. Our client never tries it; noted so nobody is surprised.
  • The webhook key name is fixed in YAML. LiveKit signs webhooks with the key named in livekit.home.yaml, which cannot read .env. The guide now says: name the key yappa. A mismatch costs only the event log lines.
  • First attempt failed on a self-made bug: the spike created invite codes with capitals, the server lowercases codes before the lookup. Fixed in the spike; the server behaviour (codes are case-insensitive) is intended.

Decision it feeds

  • ADR-002 revisit trigger "S6 overruns → PocketBase": not triggered. The control plane stays Rust.
  • ADR-005 confirmed by measurement: presence in the LiveKit room, control plane HTTP only, webhook for the log.
  • No new ADR. Two implementation decisions recorded here and in crates/control: bootstrap and emergency via the binary's subcommands instead of a web page; kick = out of every room now (TeamSpeak-style), the account stays. Every request carries x-yappa-version, so the minimum version also blocks token requests, not only logins.

Follow-up tasks (also in TASKS.md)

  • C1: PresenceLink builds its map from remote_participants() at connect plus attribute, connect and disconnect events; reconnects re-read the full list.
  • Phase 2: show a person as "maybe gone" when their presence connection is stale (no attribute or heartbeat change, voice silent) instead of waiting for LiveKit's 20 s.
  • The VPS compose (vps.yml) reuses the control service and the Caddy /api/ route from home.yml.
  • lk load-test with 20 publishers plus 20 presence clients.
